Revised take incorporating SLOOS: The December 14, 2022 FOMC message remains clearly hawkish and credibility-focused (4.25–4.50% funds rate, 4.4% IOER, 4.3% ON RRP, and ongoing QT), with explicit attention to lags, cumulative tightening, and data dependence. Layering in the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey points to a materially tighter credit backdrop than the statement alone implies:

- Banks reported tightening standards across C&I (including foreign banks) and CRE (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily), with residential mortgage categories also tightening (QM jumbo, non-QM jumbo, subprime) and consumer credit conditions tighter (credit cards and broader consumer loans), while auto standards were largely unchanged.
- Loan demand weakened notably from large, middle-market, and small firms, and softened for credit cards and autos; HELOC demand strengthened. Banks cited the economic outlook and customer needs as key drivers.
- Approval standards shifted up the credit spectrum (less likely to approve at FICO 620/680, more likely at 720), and banks reported an increased likelihood of recession.

Implications: SLOOS suggests additional endogenous tightening in financial conditions that will amplify the restrictive stance and weigh more heavily on growth and risk assets, with particular vigilance warranted in CRE. This raises near-term downside risks beyond a plain reading of the FOMC statement, even as core banking resilience supports policy credibility over the medium term.

Net effect: more negative than before given tighter credit supply and weaker demand across firms and consumers.
